Matt Cox, Matson's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, commented, "Matson had a stronger-than-expected third quarter. Our China service performed well, with its speed and reliability serving as important differentiators amid continued pressure on global shipping networks and congestion at key Asia ports. Strong demand and elevated freight rates in our China service drove a substantial year-over-year increase in Ocean Transportation operating income, particularly compared with last year's muted peak season. In our domestic ocean tradelanes and logistics, we saw stable performance."
Revenue growth

A company’s long-term performance is an indicator of its overall quality. Any business can deliver a good quarter or two, but many enduring ones grow for years. Matson’s revenue grew at a sluggish 1.9% compounded annual growth rate over the last five years, falling short of our standards.

Long-term growth matters most, but within industrials, a half-decade historical view may miss new industry trends or demand cycles. Matson’s annualized revenue growth of 5.5% over the last two years is above its five-year trend, a positive sign.
This quarter, Matson reported strong year-on-year revenue growth of 26.5%, and its $1.11 billion in revenue topped Wall Street’s consensus estimates by 4.3%.

Looking ahead, sell-side analysts expect revenue to remain flat over the next 12 months, according to S&P, a deceleration versus the last two years. This projection is underwhelming and indicates its products and services will see some demand headwinds.
Operating margin
Operating margin is a key measure of profitability. Think of it as net income, the bottom line, excluding the impact of taxes and interest on debt, which are less connected to business fundamentals.

Matson has operated efficiently over the last five years. It demonstrated high profitability for an industrials business, with an average operating margin of 19.6%. This result was particularly impressive given its low gross margin, which largely reflects what it sells and requires substantial changes to move meaningfully. Companies have more control over their operating margins, and high operating margins alongside low gross margins indicate well-managed operations.

Looking at the trend in its profitability, Matson’s operating margin decreased by 17.8 percentage points over the last five years. This raises questions about the company’s expense base because its revenue growth should have given it leverage on its fixed costs, resulting in better economies of scale and profitability.

This quarter, Matson generated an operating margin of 22.9%, up 5.2 percentage points year on year. The increase was solid, and its operating margin rose more than its gross margin, indicating greater efficiency in expenses such as marketing, research and development and administrative overhead.
Earnings per share

Revenue trends explain a company’s historical growth, but the long-term change in earnings per share, or EPS, points to the profitability of that growth. For example, a company could inflate its revenue through excessive spending on advertising and promotions.

Matson’s EPS grew at a 4.5% compounded annual growth rate over the last five years. This performance was better than its revenue growth but doesn’t tell us much about its business quality because its operating margin improvement lagged that of peers.

A closer look at Matson’s earnings helps explain the drivers of its performance. A five-year view shows that Matson has repurchased its stock, shrinking its share count by 30.6%. This indicates its EPS outperformed its revenue not because of increased operational efficiency but financial engineering, as buybacks boost
per
share earnings.
Like with revenue, we analyze EPS over a shorter period to see if we are missing a change in the business.
For Matson, its two-year annual EPS growth of 21.3% was higher than its five-year trend. This acceleration made it one of the faster-growing industrials companies in recent history.

In Q3, Matson reported EPS of $6.96, up from $4.24 in the same quarter last year. EPS topped analysts’ consensus estimates by a wide margin, a positive result for shareholders. Over the next 12 months, Wall Street expects Matson’s full-year EPS to shrink by 1.7% from $17.68 to $17.37, according to S&P.
Key takeaways from Matson’s Q3 results
Matson delivered a solid Q3, beating both EBITDA and revenue consensus estimates by wide margins. Those were the quarter’s key positives. Shares rose 3.9% to $219.94 immediately after the results.

Matson had a positive quarter, but one earnings result doesn’t necessarily make the stock a buy. The latest quarter is only one piece of the longer-term business quality picture. Quality, combined with valuation, can help determine whether the stock is a buy.
